title.en: Mitral stenosis: the tight rheumatic valve

idea.en: Recognise doming leaflets, a fish mouth orifice and left atrial enlargement of mitral stenosis.

alt.en: Parasternal long axis shows doming of the anterior mitral leaflet with a small diastolic opening and an enlarged left atrium.

steps.en: What you see: The mitral leaflets look thick and bright. In diastole the anterior leaflet domes like an open parachute while the tips stay stuck together. In short axis the closed tips form a small fish mouth opening. The left atrium is enlarged and may show slow swirling smoke like spontaneous contrast. In long standing disease the right side enlarges and the pulmonary trunk looks prominent.

Normal values with units: Mitral valve area by planimetry. Normal 4 to 6 sq cm. Mild stenosis above 1.5 sq cm. Moderate 1.0 to 1.5 sq cm. Severe below 1.0 sq cm.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on mitral stenosis quantitation

Mean transmitral gradient. Mild below 5 mmHg. Moderate 5 to 10 mmHg. Severe above 10 mmHg at a normal heart rate.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on mitral stenosis quantitation

Pressure half time. Severe 220 ms or more. Valve area in sq cm equals 220 divided by the pressure half time in ms.. Source: ASE and EACVI 2017 valvular stenosis guideline, section on mitral stenosis quantitation
Left atrial volume index. Normal 34 ml per sq m or below. Above this, the atrium is enlarged.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left atrial volume

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: In sinus rhythm the P wave is broad and notched in lead two from left atrial enlargement. Atrial fibrillation is common once the atrium enlarges. Right axis or right ventricular hypertrophy appears when pulmonary pressure rises.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: The first sound is loud while the leaflets stay mobile. An opening snap follows the second sound in early diastole. A low pitched mid diastolic rumble is best heard at the apex with the patient lying on the left side.

spot.en: Landmarks: Anterior mitral leaflet with diastolic doming
Fused leaflet tips forming the fish mouth orifice
Enlarged left atrium behind the aortic root
Interventricular septum and aortic root for orientation
What to report: Valve area by planimetry with the mean gradient and heart rate at the time
Pressure half time and left atrial volume index
Pulmonary pressure estimate and right heart size
Rhythm on the ECG and any left atrial smoke or clot
Red flags needing urgent referral: Atrial fibrillation with a fast rate or any embolic event, needs urgent rate control and anticoagulation review
Pulmonary oedema or haemoptysis with severe stenosis, needs urgent cardiology review
Signs of pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure, needs urgent referral
Pitfalls: Tachycardia raises the gradient, so note the heart rate and repeat when the rate is controlled.
Mitral regurgitation through the same valve raises flow and the gradient, so grade regurgitation separately.
Left atrial smoke can hide a clot, so sweep the whole atrium and appendage slowly.
Figure: Parasternal short axis at mitral level shows the fish mouth orifice. Planimeter the smallest opening in mid diastole at maximal opening. View tte_psax_mv

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Place the patient on the left side and start with the parasternal long axis at the left sternal edge.
Centre the mitral valve and reduce depth so the left atrium fills the far field.
Freeze in mid diastole at maximal opening and watch the anterior leaflet dome while the tips stay together.
Sweep to the short axis at mitral level and find the smallest fish mouth opening.
Put colour over the valve to show the narrow diastolic jet and any atrial smoke.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Cutting too basal so the leaflets look thick and the orifice looks smaller than it is. Fix: Move the probe one space down toward the apex and angle back toward the base until both leaflets and the left atrium appear.
Measuring the orifice in systole when the valve is closed. Fix: Wait for mid diastole on the moving image and planimeter the frame with the widest tip separation.
Reading colour mosaic as severe stenosis when colour gain is set too high. Fix: Lower colour gain until background noise just disappears, then confirm the jet in two views.

q.en: Which finding marks rheumatic mitral stenosis in short axis?

o.en: A prolapsing leaflet with a posterior jet
A fish mouth opening with doming leaflets

why.en: Commissural fusion leaves a small fish mouth opening and the anterior leaflet domes in diastole.

q.en: Which valve area means severe mitral stenosis?

why.en: Severe is below 1.0 sq cm with a mean gradient above 10 mmHg at a normal heart rate.

q.en: A young patient has severe mitral stenosis. What fits the Indian context?

o.en: Rheumatic heart disease is common in India, so ask about sore throat history and refer for secondary prophylaxis assessment
Mitral stenosis is always degenerative, so no history is needed
Antibiotics cure the fused commissures, so echo follow up is not needed

why.en: Rheumatic heart disease is common in India and recurrent rheumatic fever drives progression, so secondary prophylaxis review matters.
